|website={{url|weareprogressives.org}} |country=United States }} The '''Congressional Progressive Caucus''' ('''CPC''') is a [[Congressional caucus|membership organization]] within the [[United States Democratic Party|Democratic]] [[congressional caucus]] in the [[United States Congress]].{{cite web|url=https://cpc-grijalva.house.gov/caucus-members/|title=Congressional Progressive Caucus: Caucus Members|work=house.gov}} The CPC is a [[left-leaning]] organization that works to advance [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]] and [[Modern liberalism in the United States|liberal]] issues and positions and represents the [[Factions in the Democratic Party (United States)|progressive faction]] of the Democratic Party.{{cite book|publisher=Beacon Press|isbn=978-0807043172|title=Mobilizing Resentment: Conservative Resurgence From The John Birch Society To The Promise Keepers|last=Hardisty|first=Jean|location=Boston, MA.|year=2000|page=221}}{{cite web|title=Two congressmen endorse Carl Sciortino in race to replace Markey in Congress|url=http://www.boston.com/yourtown/news/medford/2013/09/two_congressmen_endorse_carl_sciortino_in_race_to_replace_ma.html|publisher=[[Boston.com]]|accessdate=July 23, 2014|date=September 13, 2013}} "[T]he Congressional Progressive Caucus, the umbrella group for left-leaning Democratic members of Congress". It was founded in 1991 and has grown steadily since then, having more recently added 20 members since 2005 and having hired its first full-time Executive Director, Bill Goold, in May of that year. Subsequent Executive Directors have included Andrea Miller (2009–2011) and Brad Bauman (2011–2014). With 78 members, it is currently the largest Democratic congressional caucus. The CPC is currently co-chaired by U.S. Representatives [[Raúl Grijalva]] (D-AZ) and [[Mark Pocan]] (D-WI). The current Executive Director is Mike Darner. Of the 20 [[List of United States House committees|standing committees of the House]] in the [[111th United States Congress|111th Congress]], 10 were chaired by members of the CPC. Those chairmen were replaced when the Republicans took control of the House in the [[112th United States Congress|112th Congress]]. == History == The CPC was established in 1991 by six members of the [[United States House of Representatives]], namely U.S. Representatives [[Ron Dellums]] (D-CA), [[Lane Evans]] (D-IL), [[Thomas Andrews (politician)|Thomas Andrews]] (D-ME), [[Peter DeFazio]] (D-OR), [[Maxine Waters]] (D-CA) and [[Bernie Sanders]] (I-VT). Additional House Members joined soon thereafter, including [[Major Owens]] (D-NY), [[Nydia Velázquez]] (D-NY), [[David Bonior]] (D-MI), [[Bob Filner]] (D-CA), [[Barney Frank]] (D-MA), [[Maurice Hinchey]] (D-NY), [[Jim McDermott]] (D-WA), [[Jerrold Nadler]] (D-NY), [[Patsy Mink]] (D-HI), [[George Miller (California politician)|George Miller]] (D-CA), [[Pete Stark]] (D-CA), [[John Olver]] (D-MA), [[Lynn Woolsey]] (D-CA) and [[Nancy Pelosi]] (D-CA). Sanders was the convener and first CPC Chairman. Bill Goold served as Staff Coordinator for the Progressive Caucus in its early years until 1998. The founding CPC members were concerned about the economic hardship imposed by the deepening recession and the growing inequality brought about by the timidity of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] response in the early 1990s. On January 3, 1995 at a standing room only news conference on Capitol Hill, they were the first group inside Congress to chart a detailed, comprehensive legislative alternative to U.S. Speaker Newt Gingrich and the Republican [[Contract with America]], which they termed "the most regressive tax proposals and reactionary social legislation the Congress had before it in 70 years". The CPC's ambitious agenda was framed as "The Progressive Promise: Fairness". === Budget proposal for 2012 === In April 2011, the Congressional Progressive Caucus released a proposed "People's Budget" for fiscal year 2012.{{cite web|title=The People's Budget|publisher=Congressional Progressive Caucus|url=http://grijalva.house.gov/uploads/The%20CPC%20FY2012%20Budget.pdf|accessdate=April 24, 2011}} Two of its proponents stated: "By implementing a fair tax code, by building a resilient American economy, and by bringing our troops home, we achieve a budget surplus of over $30 billion by 2021 and we end up with a debt that is less than 65% of our GDP. This is what sustainability looks like".{{citation|last=Honda|first=Michael|author-link=Michael Honda|last2=Grijalva|first2=Raul|author2-link=Raul Grijalva|title=The only real Democratic budget|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=April 11, 2011|url=http://thehill.com/blogs/congress-blog/economy-a-budget/155221-the-only-real-democratic-budget|accessdate=March 24, 2018}} == Ideology == The CPC advocates "universal access to affordable, high quality healthcare" ([[universal healthcare]] or [[single-payer healthcare]]), [[fair trade]] agreements, [[living wage]] laws, the right of all workers to organize into [[trade union|labor unions]] and engage in [[collective bargaining]], the abolition of the [[USA PATRIOT Act]], the legalization of [[same-sex marriage]], U.S. participation in international treaties such as the climate change related [[Kyoto Accords]], strict [[campaign finance reform]] laws, a crackdown on [[corporate welfare]] and influence, an increase in [[income tax]] rates on upper-middle and upper class households, [[tax cuts]] for the poor and an increase in [[Social welfare|welfare]] spending by the federal government.{{cite web|publisher=Congressional Progressive Caucus|title=The Progressive Promise|accessdate=September 28, 2018|url=https://cpc-grijalva.house.gov/the-progressive-promise/}} == List of Chairs == {|class="wikitable" !Term start !Term end !colspan=2|Chair(s) |- |1991 |1999 |colspan=2|
